summary: A threat actor added a malicious version of a SolarWinds Orion library to the vendor's build process, signed with SolarWinds' own certificate. Customers who installed the updates ran a backdoor. CISA described follow-on activity in government and private networks.

overview.background: SolarWinds Orion is network monitoring software with high privileges in customer networks. CISA says compromises date back to at least March 2020.
systems: Signed Orion updates (versions 2019.4 HF5 to 2020.2 HF1)
Identity systems such as SAML signing certificates
overview.impact: U.S. government agencies, critical infrastructure and private organisations were compromised, per CISA.
overview.severity: Severe. CISA issued Emergency Directive 21-01 on 13 December 2020.
overview.gaps: The alert covers detection and mitigation. It does not give a full timeline of the intrusion.

archNote: Components and relationships come from the cited source where it describes them. Layout and labels are ours.

diagrams.title: Trusted update delivers a backdoor
diagrams.caption: Per CISA, the actor added a malicious DLL to the build process, signed with SolarWinds' legitimate certificate; the backdoor beaconed to a victim-specific domain.

diagrams.title: Defending the build and the network (conceptual)
diagrams.caption: Controls that reduce the chance and impact of a poisoned update. Not from CISA's alert in detail.

afterChanges: Management software cannot call the internet freely.
afterNote: The after picture shows the corrective ideas in the source and general good practice. It is conceptual unless the source says otherwise.
timelineNote: Times are as published by the source. Entries without a clock time are given in order only.

timeline.e: CISA reports the earliest known compromises.
Compromised updates reach customers and the actor operates in some networks.
CISA issues Emergency Directive 21-01 ordering agencies to disconnect affected devices.
Partners redirect the command domain to a Microsoft-blocklisted address.
Update with mitigations and indicators; organisations rebuild Orion and rotate credentials.

rootCause.trigger: The actor compromised the SolarWinds build process and added a malicious DLL.
rootCause.underlying: It was signed with the vendor's certificate, so it looked legitimate to customers.
contributing: Other access methods such as password spraying and stolen keys were also used
Identity systems such as SAML signing were abused

evidence.label: The build tampering
evidence.body: added a malicious version of the binary solarwinds.orion.core.businesslayer.dll

evidence.label: Update advice
evidence.body: installing all updates within 48 hours of release
evidence.note: From CISA's alert; CISA's general advice.

evidence.label: A simulated Orion version check
evidence.note: Where a version might be read. Illustrative, not from CISA.

diagnose.step: Find all Orion servers and versions.
diagnose.why: Compare with the listed affected versions.

diagnose.step: Look for the indicators CISA lists.
Classify the network by evidence of follow-on activity.

correct.step: Disconnect or power down affected instances.

verify.step: Check no traffic to the command domain.

prevent.step: Plan incident response out of band.

fix.safety: A full rebuild of the identity environment may be needed. Plan it, do not improvise.

troubleshoot.scenario: A vendor's signed update turns out to be malicious. It runs on a server that can reach everything.
troubleshoot.question: What do you do?
troubleshoot.answer: Isolate, block the command domain, rebuild from trusted sources, rotate credentials and review identity and logs out of band.

rootcause.q: What made the update look legitimate?
options: It was signed with the vendor's certificate

remediation.answer: Management servers may reach only update hosts.

design.prompt: Design update trust for monitoring tools.
design.answer: Staging, hash checks, egress control, least privilege and monitoring of behaviour.

checks.q: Per CISA, how long should logs be retained?
Was Orion the only initial access method?
What did CISA advise for updates?

sources.title: CISA: Advanced Persistent Threat Compromise of Government Agencies, Critical Infrastructure, and Private Sector Organizations (AA20-352A)
